a: Design that ensures products address the needs of the widest possible audience regardless of age or ability, breaking down barriers so experiences are usable by everyone. It extends UCD to forgotten groups such as pregnant, elderly, disabled or injured people.

q: Give the Center for Universal Design definition of universal design.
a: The design of products and environments to be usable by all people, to the greatest extent possible, without the need for adaptation or specialized design.

q: Distinguish accessible, inclusive and universal design.
a: Accessible: removes barriers so disabled people can use it (often a legal minimum). Inclusive: mainstream design for as many people as possible, with diverse users involved. Universal: the ideal of one design usable by all without adaptation.

q: Why is universal design not the same as one size fits all?
a: It aims to accommodate a variety of users, often through flexibility, adjustability and multi-sensory information, rather than forcing one fixed solution on everyone.

q: Who coined universal design and when? What conflict exists?
a: Architect Ronald L. Mace. NC State, citing Bess Williamson, dates it to 1985. Metcalfe writes Ron Mace (1998). The seven principles date from 1997.

q: List the seven principles of universal design.
a: Equitable use; flexibility in use; simple and intuitive use; perceptible information; tolerance for error; low physical effort; size and space for approach and use.

q: Name three national disability laws listed in Metcalfe.
a: Any three: Australia Disability Discrimination Act 1992; Ontarians with Disabilities Act 2001; Americans with Disabilities Act 1990; South Africa PEPUDA 2000; India Persons with Disabilities Act 1995.

q: How is disability addressed in developing countries without formal legislation?
a: Through informal guidelines and international standards promoted by NGOs and government agencies.

q: Give three everyday examples of inclusive currency design.
a: Coins of different size, thickness and edge detail; notes of different sizes, colours and textures; raised dots on polymer banknotes (Australia, Canada, UK); intaglio printing; AI note-reader apps.

q: Why is there no truly average person?
a: Body dimensions are not linearly correlated: someone with short arms does not necessarily have short legs. Designing for the 50th percentile excludes many people, especially across several dimensions.

q: What three strategies help designers accommodate a wider range of users (C1.2.2)?
a: Use comprehensive anthropometric data; add adjustable features; identify specific user groups (gender, age, limitations) and tailor the design, usually covering the 5th to 95th percentile.

q: Which percentile is used for minimum reach, and which for doorway clearance?
a: Reach (and operating force): 5th percentile, so the smallest or weakest can manage. Clearance: 95th percentile, so the largest fit.

q: What did the 1850 Union soldier data show?
a: Soldiers aged 21-49 averaged 5 ft 8 in (about 1.73 m). Few if any were exactly average, but the full distribution was useful for sizing clothing and weapons.
Developing solutions for users with physical, sensory and cognitive impairments that also suit the general population.

q: List four advantages of designing for extremes.
a: Any four: benefits a wider audience; innovative solutions; future-proof designs; better user experience for all; inspiration to rethink assumptions; improved accessibility.

q: Describe the OXO Good Grips peeler as a design for extremes.
a: Inspired by Sam Farber's wife's arthritis: an oversized non-slip Santoprene handle with a finned soft spot needing only a light grip, and a swivel stainless-steel blade. Comfortable for everyone; entered MoMA in 1994.

q: How did the Xbox Adaptive Controller (announced 16 May 2018) apply inclusive design?
a: Co-developed with AbleGamers, the Cerebral Palsy Foundation, Craig Hospital, SpecialEffect and Warfighter Engaged for gamers with limited mobility. It has two large reprogrammable buttons and works with existing adaptive switches, at USD 99.99.

q: What does the WHO estimate about disability (fact sheet, 7 March 2023)?
a: About 1.3 billion people, 16 percent of the world's population or 1 in 6, have a significant disability, and the number is growing as populations age and noncommunicable diseases rise.

q: Give two reasons inclusive design is not always possible.
a: Any two: cost; conflicting needs of different user groups; technical limits; safety requirements; the 5th-95th range still excludes about 10 percent.
